Predicting Employee Attrition: A Machine Learning Approach¶

Work completed by:

  • Castro Freibott, Rodrigo

  • del Mazo Vázquez, Juan

Employee attrition and burnout represent critical challenges for organizations, directly impacting productivity, morale, and costs. This work leverages machine learning techniques to predict employee attrition, offering valuable insights to support human resource management decisions.

The analysis is systematically structured into multiple stages. It begins with exploratory data analysis (EDA) to understand the dataset and identify key patterns. This is followed by comprehensive preprocessing to address data quality issues, such as missing values and class imbalance. Basic and advanced machine learning models are then implemented, with hyperparameter optimization to enhance performance. Finally, the best-performing model is applied to predict employee attrition on a competition dataset, simulating its deployment in a real-world scenario.

By integrating robust methodologies and advanced techniques, this project aims to deliver a high-quality predictive model while emphasizing reproducibility, interpretability, and practical applicability in the field of human resource analytics.

The approach ensures that the Python code is executed sequentially as it is read, avoiding the unnecessary repetition of blocks such as library imports in multiple sections. This structure enhances the readability, organization, and efficiency of the code, ensuring a smooth flow for interpretation and execution. Furthermore, the sections are arranged to provide a clear and logical understanding of the concepts, methodologies, and results.

1. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) of Employee Attrition Dataset¶

Introduction:

The Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) step is critical in understanding the structure, quality, and potential challenges in the dataset. This process helps identify patterns, anomalies, and relationships among features that will guide preprocessing and modeling decisions. Specifically, in this task, the EDA aims to:

  1. Determine the number of instances and features in the dataset.

  2. Differentiate between categorical and numerical variables.

  3. Identify missing values and evaluate their impact.

  4. Detect constant columns and potential ID columns.

  5. Analyze the distribution of the target variable (Attrition) and check for class imbalance.

  6. Evaluate high cardinality in categorical variables, which can influence feature engineering decisions.

  7. Check for duplicate rows that might affect the integrity of the data.

The findings from this step will serve as the foundation for designing robust preprocessing and modeling pipelines.

In [1]:
# Import necessary libraries
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Set seed for reproducibility (student ID of Juan del Mazo Vázquez)
STUDENT_ID = 123456789
np.random.seed(STUDENT_ID)

# Load the dataset
data = pd.read_csv('attrition_availabledata_10.csv')
print("Dataset loaded successfully!")

# Display dataset shape (number of rows and columns)
print("Shape of the dataset:", data.shape)

# Show column types
print("\nData types of each column:")
print(data.dtypes)

# Identify categorical and numerical columns
categorical_columns = data.select_dtypes(include=['object']).columns
numerical_columns = data.select_dtypes(include=['number']).columns

print("\nCategorical columns:", categorical_columns.tolist())
print("Numerical columns:", numerical_columns.tolist())

# Check for missing values
missing_values = data.isnull().sum()
missing_values = missing_values[missing_values > 0]
print("\nMissing values per column:")
print(missing_values)

# Identify columns with constant values
constant_columns = [col for col in data.columns if data[col].nunique() <= 1]
print("\nConstant columns (if any):", constant_columns)

# Identify potential ID columns (high cardinality with unique values)
potential_id_columns = [col for col in data.columns if data[col].nunique() == data.shape[0]]
print("\nPotential ID columns (unique for every row):", potential_id_columns)

# Analyze the target variable (if it exists)
if 'Attrition' in data.columns:
    target_counts = data['Attrition'].value_counts(normalize=True)
    print("\nTarget variable distribution:")
    print(target_counts)
    if target_counts.min() < 0.4:  # Arbitrary threshold for imbalance
        print("The dataset is imbalanced.")
    else:
        print("The dataset is balanced.")

# Analyze cardinality of categorical variables
print("\nCategorical variables with high cardinality:")
for col in categorical_columns:
    unique_values = data[col].nunique()
    if unique_values > 10:  # Arbitrary threshold for high cardinality
        print(f"- {col}: {unique_values} unique values")

# Additional analysis: Check for duplicate rows
duplicate_rows = data.duplicated().sum()
print(f"\nNumber of duplicate rows in the dataset: {duplicate_rows}")

# Summary of the analysis
print("\nEDA Summary:")
print(f"- Total instances: {data.shape[0]}")
print(f"- Total features: {data.shape[1]}")
print(f"- Numerical features: {len(numerical_columns)}")
print(f"- Categorical features: {len(categorical_columns)}")
print(f"- Missing values: {missing_values.sum()} in columns: {missing_values[missing_values > 0].index.tolist()}")
print(f"- Constant features: {len(constant_columns)}")
print(f"- Potential ID columns: {len(potential_id_columns)}")
print(f"- Duplicate rows: {duplicate_rows}")
print(f"- Problem type: {'Classification' if 'Attrition' in data.columns else 'Unknown'}")

High Cardinality in Categorical Variables:

Column Unique Values
None Identified N/A

  • No categorical variables have more than 10 unique values, based on the threshold used for high cardinality.

    • This threshold was chosen because variables with more than 10 unique values can lead to high dimensionality when using One-Hot Encoding.

  • Since no variables exceed the threshold, encoding can proceed with standard techniques like One-Hot Encoding, ensuring efficient preprocessing without requiring advanced techniques like Target Encoding.

Correlation Analysis: Heatmap Visualization

In [5]:
import seaborn as sns

# Filter numerical columns from the dataset
numerical_data = data[numerical_columns]  # Select only numerical columns

# Calculate correlation matrix
correlation_matrix = numerical_data.corr()

# Plot the heatmap
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))
sns.heatmap(correlation_matrix, annot=True, cmap="coolwarm", fmt=".2f", linewidths=0.5)
plt.title("Correlation Heatmap of Numerical Features")
plt.show()

  • Low Correlation Across Most Features: The majority of features have weak or negligible correlations (values close to 0). This indicates that many features are independent and capture unique information.

  • Significant Correlations:

    • YearsWithCurrManager and YearsAtCompany (0.77): Strong positive correlation. Employees with longer tenures at the company tend to work longer with the same manager.

    • PerformanceRating and PercentSalaryHike (0.77): Strong positive correlation, showing employees with higher performance ratings tend to receive larger salary hikes.

    • TotalWorkingYears and Age (0.68); TotalWorkingYears and YearsAtCompany (0.64): Positive correlation, showing employees that have been working for longer tend to be older and have spent more time working at the company.

  • Weak or Negligible Correlations:

    • MonthlyIncome and TotalWorkingYears (-0.03): Virtually no linear relationship between these features.

    • PerformanceRating and other features: Aside from its correlation with PercentSalaryHike, it shows little to no correlation with other attributes.

  • Multicollinearity or Redundancy: High correlation between YearsWithCurrManager and YearsAtCompany (0.77) suggests potential multicollinearity. We can consider dropping or transforming one of these features.

Outlier Detection: Systematic Detection

In [6]:
outlier_summary = {}
for col in numerical_columns:
    Q1 = data[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = data[col].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    outliers = data[(data[col] < Q1 - 1.5 * IQR) | (data[col] > Q3 + 1.5 * IQR)]
    outlier_summary[col] = len(outliers)

# Display outlier counts
print(outlier_summary)

2. Setup¶

2.1. Outer Evaluation¶

Test set creation:

  • Chosen Size: 20% of the dataset (588 samples) has been allocated for the test set.

  • Reasoning:

    • Standard Practice: The 80-20 split is a commonly used approach in machine learning, balancing the need for sufficient training data and a reliable evaluation set.

    • Robust Evaluation: A 20% test set ensures a sufficient number of samples (588) to evaluate model performance effectively.

    • Training Data: The remaining 80% (2,352 samples) provides ample data for training robust models.

  • Stratification: This approach ensures that the class distribution of the target variable (Attrition) is preserved in both training and test sets, which is especially important for this imbalanced dataset.

    • The original dataset has a highly imbalanced target variable:

      • 83.88% of the samples are in the "No" class (employees who did not leave).

      • 16.12% of the samples are in the "Yes" class (employees who left).

    • Stratified splitting ensures that these proportions are maintained in both the training and test sets, leading to a fair and consistent evaluation of models.

In addition, we need to remove the constant and ID columns identified earlier.

In [10]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Remove constant and ID columns
print(f"Columns before removing constant and ID columns: {data.shape[1]}")
constant_columns = ['EmployeeCount', 'Over18', 'StandardHours']
id_columns = ['EmployeeID']
data_cleaned = data.drop(columns=constant_columns + id_columns)
print(f"Columns after removing constant and ID columns: {data_cleaned.shape[1]}")

# Separate features (X) and target (y)
X = data_cleaned.drop(columns='Attrition')  # Features
y = data_cleaned['Attrition']               # Target

# Split the data into train (80%) and test (20%) sets, maintaining class distribution
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=STUDENT_ID
)

# Print train-test split sizes
print(f"Train set size: {X_train.shape}")
print(f"Test set size: {X_test.shape}")

Columns before removing constant and ID columns: 31
Columns after removing constant and ID columns: 27
Train set size: (2352, 26)
Test set size: (588, 26)

  • Train Set Size: 2,352 samples

  • Test Set Size: 588 samples

  • The test set will remain unused until the final model is developed and selected, ensuring unbiased performance estimation.

2.2. Inner Evaluation¶

Chosen Method: 5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation

Why 5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation?

  1. Class Imbalance:

    • Stratified k-fold cross-validation ensures that the class distribution of the target variable (Attrition) is preserved across all folds.

    • This is critical for datasets with severe class imbalance, like this one, where the "Yes" class represents only 16.12% of the data.

  2. Reliable Estimates:

    • A 5-fold split strikes a balance between computational efficiency and robust performance evaluation.

    • It ensures that each data point is used for both training and validation, providing consistent and reliable metrics.

  3. Fair Evaluation:

    • Each fold acts as both a training and validation set, ensuring that the models are evaluated impartially.

Purpose of Inner Evaluation:

  1. Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO):

    • The inner evaluation will tune hyperparameters for selected models to maximize performance on validation folds.

  2. Algorithm Selection (CASH):

    • It will compare multiple machine learning algorithms to identify the best-performing model. This addresses the CASH problem (Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization).

Evaluation Metrics:

  1. Accuracy: Represents the overall proportion of correct predictions. However, due to the class imbalance, this metric might be overly influenced by the majority class.

  2. Balanced Accuracy: Provides a more equitable metric by averaging recall for both the majority and minority classes.

  3. Training Time: Measures the computational cost of training, which is crucial for scalability in real-world applications.

Implementation Plan:

  • Cross-Validation Setup:

    • During hyperparameter tuning and model comparison, a 5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation will be used.

    • Each fold will preserve the class distribution, ensuring fair evaluation of both the majority and minority classes.

  • Metrics Usage:

    • Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, and Training Time will be reported for all folds to guide the selection of the best model and hyperparameters.

  • Connection to Outer Evaluation:

    • The test set (outer evaluation) will remain unused until the final model is selected, ensuring unbiased performance estimation on unseen data.
In [12]:
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold

inner = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=STUDENT_ID)

3. Exploring and Optimizing Basic Methods: Decision Trees and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)¶

3.1. Decision Trees and KNN with Default Hyperparameters¶

Introduction:

The objective of this section is to:

  1. Train, evaluate, and compare Decision Trees and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and a Dummy Classifier to establish baseline performance using default hyperparameters.

  2. Analyze the performance of these models using key metrics: Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, Execution Time, and Confusion Matrices.

  3. Ensure reproducibility and clarity in results presentation, following the assignment's general considerations.

Preprocessing:

To prepare the data for training, a preprocessing pipeline is created to handle:

  • Missing values: Numerical features are imputed with the mean, and categorical features are imputed with the mode.

  • Scaling: Numerical features are standardized to have zero mean and unit variance.

  • Encoding: Categorical features are encoded to turn them into numeric data.

    • One-hot encoding: for nominal features.
    • Ordinal encoding: for ordinal features.

In principle, decision trees do not need scaling or one-hot encoding. However, their performance is unaffected by scaling, and scikit-learn's implementation of trees only supports numerical features so it needs one-hot encoding: https://scikit-learn.org/1.5/modules/tree.html#tree

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder

print("Original data (first rows):\n", X_train.head(10).to_string())
print()

# Distinguish between categorical features: ordinal and nominal
categorical_ordinal = {
    'BusinessTravel': ['Non-Travel', 'Travel_Rarely', 'Travel_Frequently']
}
categorical_nominal = [feature for feature in categorical_features if feature not in categorical_ordinal.keys()]

# Preprocessing for numerical features: Imputation and Scaling
numerical_transformer = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('imputer', SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')),  # Replace missing values with the mean
    ('scaler', StandardScaler())  # Standardize numerical features
])

# Preprocessing for ordinal categorical features: Imputation and Ordinal Encoding
ordinal_transformers = []
for feature, categories in categorical_ordinal.items():
    ordinal_transformers.append((
        feature,
        Pipeline(steps=[
            ('imputer', SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent')),  # Replace missing values with the mode
            ('ordinal', OrdinalEncoder(categories=[categories]))  # Ordinal encode the feature
        ]),
        [feature]
    ))

# Preprocessing for nominal categorical features: Imputation and One-Hot Encoding
nominal_transformer = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('imputer', SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent')),  # Replace missing values with the mode
    ('onehot', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'))  # One-hot encode nominal categorical features
])

# Combine preprocessors into a single ColumnTransformer
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ('num', numerical_transformer, numerical_features),
        *ordinal_transformers,
        ('cat', nominal_transformer, categorical_nominal)
    ]
)

# Apply preprocessing pipeline and show columns and first rows
X_train_transformed = preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train)
nominal_columns = preprocessor.named_transformers_['cat']['onehot'].get_feature_names_out(categorical_nominal)
transformed_columns = numerical_features + list(categorical_ordinal.keys()) + nominal_columns.tolist()
X_train_transformed_df = pd.DataFrame(X_train_transformed, columns=transformed_columns)
print("Transformed data (first rows):\n", X_train_transformed_df.head(10).to_string())

Training and Evaluation with Default Hyperparameters

Three models were trained using default hyperparameters:

  1. Decision Tree

  2. KNN

  3. Dummy Classifier (strategy="most_frequent") as a baseline.

Metrics Reported:

  • Accuracy: Measures overall correctness of predictions.

  • Balanced Accuracy: Accounts for class imbalance, averaging recall for each class.

  • Execution Time: Evaluates computational efficiency.

  • Confusion Matrix: Provides detailed insight into prediction performance.

The metrics are computed using our choice for the inner evaluation method (explained earlier): stratified 5-fold cross-validation.

In [15]:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score, confusion_matrix
import numpy as np
import time

# Define models
dt = Pipeline(steps=[('preprocessor', preprocessor),
                     ('classifier', DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))])
knn = Pipeline(steps=[('preprocessor', preprocessor),
                      ('classifier', KNeighborsClassifier())])
dummy = Pipeline(steps=[('preprocessor', preprocessor),
                        ('classifier', DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"))])
models = {'Decision Tree': dt, 'KNN': knn, 'Dummy': dummy}

# Dictionary to store results
results_default = dict()

for model_name, model in models.items():
    accuracy_scores = []
    balanced_accuracy_scores = []
    fit_times = []
    conf_matrices = []
    
    # Perform stratified 5-fold cross-validation
    for i, (train_index, test_index) in enumerate(inner.split(X_train, y_train)):
        X_train_fold, X_test_fold = X_train.iloc[train_index], X_train.iloc[test_index]
        y_train_fold, y_test_fold = y_train.iloc[train_index], y_train.iloc[test_index]
        
        # Record fit time
        start_time = time.time()
        model.fit(X_train_fold, y_train_fold)
        fit_times.append(time.time() - start_time)
        
        # Predict and evaluate
        y_pred = model.predict(X_test_fold)
        balanced_accuracy = balanced_accuracy_score(y_test_fold, y_pred)
        accuracy_scores.append(np.mean(y_test_fold == y_pred))
        balanced_accuracy_scores.append(balanced_accuracy)
        conf_matrices.append(confusion_matrix(y_test_fold, y_pred))
        print(f"Model: {model_name} | Fold {i+1} | Balanced accuracy: {balanced_accuracy:.4f}")
    
    # Aggregate results
    results_default[model_name] = {
        'Accuracy (mean)': np.mean(accuracy_scores),
        'Accuracy (std)': np.std(accuracy_scores),
        'Balanced Accuracy (mean)': np.mean(balanced_accuracy_scores),
        'Balanced Accuracy (std)': np.std(balanced_accuracy_scores),
        'Fit Time (mean)': np.mean(fit_times),
        'Fit Time (std)': np.std(fit_times),
        'Confusion Matrix': np.sum(conf_matrices, axis=0)  # Aggregate confusion matrices across folds
    }

In [16]:
def print_results(results: dict):
    print()
    for model_name, metrics in results.items():
        print(f"Model: {model_name}")
        
        accuracy_mean = metrics.get('Accuracy (mean)', None)
        accuracy_std = metrics.get('Accuracy (std)', None)
        if accuracy_mean is not None and accuracy_std is not None:
            print(f"Accuracy (mean): {accuracy_mean:.4f} +/- {accuracy_std:.4f}")
        elif accuracy_mean is not None:
            print(f"Accuracy (mean): {accuracy_mean:.4f}")
        
        balanced_accuracy_mean = metrics.get('Balanced Accuracy (mean)', None)
        balanced_accuracy_std = metrics.get('Balanced Accuracy (std)', None)
        if balanced_accuracy_mean is not None and balanced_accuracy_std is not None:
            print(f"Balanced Accuracy (mean): {balanced_accuracy_mean:.4f} +/- {balanced_accuracy_std:.4f}")
        elif balanced_accuracy_mean is not None:
            print(f"Balanced Accuracy (mean): {balanced_accuracy_mean:.4f}")

        confusion_matrix = metrics.get('Confusion Matrix', None)
        if confusion_matrix is not None:
            print("Confusion Matrix:", confusion_matrix.tolist())
        
        fit_time_mean = metrics.get('Fit Time (mean)', None)
        fit_time_std = metrics.get('Fit Time (std)', None)
        if fit_time_mean is not None and fit_time_std is not None:
            print(f"Fit Time (mean): {fit_time_mean:.2f} +/- {fit_time_std:.4f} seconds")
        elif fit_time_mean is not None:
            print(f"Fit Time (mean): {fit_time_mean:.2f} seconds")
        
        num_candidates = metrics.get('Number of Candidates', None)
        if num_candidates is not None:
            print(f"Number of Candidates: {num_candidates}")
        
        execution_time = metrics.get('Execution Time', None)
        if execution_time is not None:
            print(f"Execution Time: {execution_time:.2f} seconds")

        best_parameters = metrics.get('Best Parameters', None)
        if best_parameters is not None:
            print(f"Best Parameters: {best_parameters}")
            
        print()


print_results(results_default)

Results:

Model Accuracy (mean) Balanced Accuracy (mean) Fit Time (mean)
Decision Tree 0.9005 ± 0.0100 0.8128 ± 0.0134 0.03 seconds
KNN 0.8478 ± 0.0071 0.5959 ± 0.0087 0.01 seconds
Dummy 0.8389 ± 0.0008 0.5000 ± 0.0000 0.01 seconds

Note: The Fit Time can vary when the code is executed again.

  1. Accuracy:

    • The Decision Tree model achieves the highest accuracy (0.9005), significantly outperforming KNN (0.8478) and the Dummy model (0.8389).
    • The Dummy model, despite its simplicity, has a comparable accuracy to KNN, indicating potential limitations in KNN's performance.

  2. Balanced Accuracy:

    • The Decision Tree model demonstrates superior balanced accuracy (0.8128), indicating it handles imbalanced data better than the other models.
    • KNN has a balanced accuracy of 0.5959, which is better than the Dummy model's baseline performance (0.5000), but still far behind the Decision Tree's performance.

  3. Efficiency:

    • In terms of fit time, the Decision Tree is the slowest (0.03 seconds), while the KNN model is as fast as the Dummy model (0.01 seconds).

  4. Overall Insights:

    • The Decision Tree model offers the best trade-off between accuracy and balanced accuracy.
    • KNN, although efficient in terms of fit time, struggles with balanced accuracy, which limits its performance in this case.
    • The Dummy model, while computationally efficient, provides baseline performance and should only be used for benchmarking purposes.

Confusion Matrices

To better understand each model's performance, we can visualize the confusion matrices aggregated across folds:

In [17]:
def plot_confusion_matrix(results, models_order=None, methods_order=None):

    # Treat "Default" as a method for comparison
    results = {k if len(k.split(" + ")) > 1 else f"{k} + Default": v for k, v in results.items()}

    base_models = set(key.split(" + ")[0] for key in results.keys())
    methods = set(key.split(" + ")[1] for key in results.keys())

    if models_order:
        base_models = [x for x in base_models if x in models_order]
        base_models = sorted(base_models, key=lambda x: models_order.index(x))
    else:
        base_models = sorted(base_models)
    if methods_order:
        methods = [x for x in methods if x in methods_order]
        methods = sorted(methods, key=lambda x: methods_order.index(x))
    else:
        methods = sorted(methods)

    model_indices = {model: idx for idx, model in enumerate(base_models)}
    method_indices = {method: idx for idx, method in enumerate(methods)}

    # Initialize the figure
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(methods), len(base_models), figsize=(6 * len(base_models), 6 * len(methods)))

    if len(methods) == 1 and len(base_models) == 1:
        axes = np.array([[axes]])  # Handle the single subplot case
    elif len(methods) == 1 or len(base_models) == 1:
        axes = np.expand_dims(axes, axis=0 if len(methods) == 1 else 1)

    for key, metrics in results.items():
        model, method = key.split(" + ")
        if model in model_indices and method in method_indices:
            ax = axes[method_indices[method], model_indices[model]]
            sns.heatmap(metrics['Confusion Matrix'], annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues', ax=ax)
            ax.set_title(f"{model} + {method}")
            ax.set_xlabel("Predicted")
            ax.set_ylabel("Actual")

    # Turn off unused subplots
    for i in range(len(methods)):
        for j in range(len(base_models)):
            if f"{base_models[j]} + {methods[i]}" not in results:
                axes[i, j].axis('off')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

plot_confusion_matrix(results_default)

Observations:

  • Decision Tree consistently outperforms KNN and Dummy models, demonstrating its suitability for this dataset.

  • KNN shows promise but struggles with class imbalance, as reflected in its lower Balanced Accuracy.

  • Dummy Classifier establishes the baseline, and all other models outperform it significantly.

3.2. Decision Trees and KNN with HPO¶

Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO):

The default hyperparameters used in the previous section are the following:

In [18]:
print("DecisionTreeClassifier default hyperparameters:")
print(DecisionTreeClassifier().get_params())

print("\nKNeighborsClassifier default hyperparameters:")
print(KNeighborsClassifier().get_params())

DecisionTreeClassifier default hyperparameters:
{'ccp_alpha': 0.0, 'class_weight': None, 'criterion': 'gini', 'max_depth': None, 'max_features': None, 'max_leaf_nodes': None, 'min_impurity_decrease': 0.0, 'min_samples_leaf': 1, 'min_samples_split': 2, 'min_weight_fraction_leaf': 0.0, 'monotonic_cst': None, 'random_state': None, 'splitter': 'best'}

KNeighborsClassifier default hyperparameters:
{'algorithm': 'auto', 'leaf_size': 30, 'metric': 'minkowski', 'metric_params': None, 'n_jobs': None, 'n_neighbors': 5, 'p': 2, 'weights': 'uniform'}

To enhance the performance of Decision Trees and KNN, we will use three hyperparameter optimization techniques:

  • GridSearch: Performs an exhaustive search over a specified parameter grid.
  • RandomizedSearch: Randomly samples from a parameter space to find the best configuration.
  • Optuna: Utilizes Bayesian optimization to efficiently explore the parameter space.

Each method will be evaluated for both computational efficiency and performance improvements.

The following subsections cover:

  • a. GridSearch Optimization: Application of GridSearch for Decision Tree and KNN, with visualizations of the grid of hyperparameter combinations covered.
  • b. RandomizedSearch Optimization: Application of RandomizedSearch for Decision Tree and KNN, with visualizations of the random hyperparameter values explored.
  • c. Optuna Optimization: Application of Optuna for Decision Tree and KNN, with visualizations of both the progress across trials and the hyperparameter values tested.
  • d. Final Comparison of HPO Methods: Comparison of the three HPO methods, presenting their results in a table and plot, and leading to concluding remarks.

a. GridSearch Optimization:¶

To identify the best hyperparameter configurations for Decision Trees and KNN using a grid-based exhaustive search approach. The Balanced Accuracy metric is used for scoring, which is particularly suitable for imbalanced datasets.

Implementation:

  • Hyperparameter Tests:

    • Decision Tree: We will tune the max_depth and min_samples_split hyperparameters.
    • KNN: We will tune the n_neighbors and weights hyperparameters.

  • Cross-Validation: Our inner evaluation process (stratified 5-fold cross-validation) is applied to assess each combination.

  • Scoring Metric: balanced_accuracy is used, to account for class imbalance.

  • Search Methodology: GridSearch systematically evaluates every combination of parameters within the defined grids.

  • Grid Expansion: The parameter grids defined in the code are not the first grids tested. The initial grid was expanded after seeing optimal hyperparameters lied at the border of the search space (e.g., the number of neighbors in KNN).

In [19]:
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

# Define models and parameter grids
models_gridsearch = {
    'Decision Tree + GridSearch': (
        dt,
        {'classifier__max_depth': [10, 20, 30, None],
        'classifier__min_samples_split': [2, 5, 10]}
    ),
    'KNN + GridSearch': (
        knn,
        {'classifier__n_neighbors': list(range(1, 8, 1)),
        'classifier__weights': ['uniform', 'distance']}
    )
}

gridsearch_cv_results = dict()
results_gridsearch = dict()
for model_name, (model, param_grid) in models_gridsearch.items():
    grid_search = GridSearchCV(model, param_grid, cv=inner, scoring='balanced_accuracy', n_jobs=-1, verbose=1)
    start_execution = time.perf_counter()
    grid_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    execution_time = time.perf_counter() - start_execution
    cv_results = grid_search.cv_results_
    best_index = grid_search.best_index_
    gridsearch_cv_results[model_name] = cv_results
    results_gridsearch[model_name] = {
        'Balanced Accuracy (mean)': cv_results['mean_test_score'][best_index],
        'Balanced Accuracy (std)': cv_results['std_test_score'][best_index],
        'Fit Time (mean)': cv_results['mean_fit_time'][best_index],
        'Fit Time (std)': cv_results['std_fit_time'][best_index],
        'Number of Candidates': len(cv_results['params']),
        'Execution Time': execution_time,
        'Best Parameters': grid_search.best_params_,
    }

print_results(results_gridsearch)

Insights:

  • Decision Tree: The hyperparameters found with GridSearch are different from the default, but they yield the same Balanced Accuracy:
    • Values:
      • GridSearch: {'max_depth': 20, 'min_samples_split': 2} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.8128)
      • Default: {'max_depth': None, 'min_samples_split': 2} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.8128)
    • Explanation: With our dataset, no tree can go beyond 20 nodes deep, so changing Max Depth beyond this value gives the same result.
  • KNN algorithm: The algorithm achieves significantly higher Balanced Accuracy with the hyperparameters found with GridSearch.
    • Values:
      • GridSearch: {'n_neighbors': 1, 'weights': 'uniform'} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.8624)
      • Default: {'n_neighbors': 5, 'weights': 'uniform'} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.5959)
    • Computational Cost: Although our results are greatly improved, the execution time is also higher (0.48 seconds with HPO, compared to 0.01 seconds without HPO).

Visualization:

The balanced accuracy scores across the evaluated parameter grid can be visualized for further insights.

For the decision tree, we will use:

b. RandomizedSearch Optimization:¶

RandomizedSearchCV is employed to optimize hyperparameters for Decision Trees and KNN by randomly sampling combinations from defined distributions. This method is particularly useful when the parameter space is large, as it reduces computational costs compared to exhaustive searches like GridSearchCV. The Balanced Accuracy metric is used for scoring, ensuring robust performance evaluation in the presence of class imbalance.

Implementation:

  • Parameter Distributions:

    • Decision Tree:

      • max_depth: Randomly sampled integers between 5 and 50.

      • min_samples_split: Randomly sampled integers between 2 and 20.

    • KNN:

      • n_neighbors: Randomly sampled integers between 1 and 20.

      • weights: Randomly chosen between uniform and distance.

  • Number of Iterations: A total of 50 random combinations are evaluated for each model.

  • Cross-Validation: 5-fold cross-validation is applied to assess parameter combinations.

  • Scoring Metric: balanced_accuracy is selected to ensure fair evaluation across classes.

In [23]:
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import randint

# Define models and parameter grids
models_randomsearch = {
    'Decision Tree + RandomSearch': (
        dt,
        {'classifier__max_depth': randint(5, 50),
         'classifier__min_samples_split': randint(2, 20)}
    ),
    'KNN + RandomSearch': (
        knn,
        {'classifier__n_neighbors': randint(1, 20),
         'classifier__weights': ['uniform', 'distance']}
    )
}

randomsearch_cv_results = dict()
results_randomsearch = dict()
for model_name, (model, param_grid) in models_randomsearch.items():
    random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
        model, param_distributions=param_grid, n_iter=50, cv=inner, scoring='balanced_accuracy', n_jobs=-1, verbose=1, random_state=STUDENT_ID
    )
    start_execution = time.perf_counter()
    random_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    execution_time = time.perf_counter() - start_execution
    cv_results = random_search.cv_results_
    best_index = random_search.best_index_
    randomsearch_cv_results[model_name] = cv_results
    results_randomsearch[model_name] = {
        'Balanced Accuracy (mean)': cv_results['mean_test_score'][best_index],
        'Balanced Accuracy (std)': cv_results['std_test_score'][best_index],
        'Fit Time (mean)': cv_results['mean_fit_time'][best_index],
        'Fit Time (std)': cv_results['std_fit_time'][best_index],
        'Number of Candidates': len(cv_results['params']),
        'Execution Time': execution_time,
        'Best Parameters': random_search.best_params_,
    }

print_results(results_randomsearch)

Insights:

  • Decision Tree: The hyperparameters found with RandomizedSearch for are different to those found with GridSearch or the default, but they all have the same Balanced Accuracy.
    • Values:
      • RandomizedSearch: {'max_depth': 47, 'min_samples_split': 2} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.8128)
      • GridSearch: {'max_depth': 20, 'min_samples_split': 2} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.8128)
      • Default: {'max_depth': None, 'min_samples_split': 2} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.8128)
    • Explanation: This strengthens our hypothesis that all values of Max Depth over 20 give identical results (when Min Samples Split is fixed to 2).
    • Computational Cost: This RandomizedSearch implementation took longer than GridSearch (1.73 seconds instead of 0.59 seconds) because we try more alternatives (50 candidates instead of 12).
  • KNN algorithm: The hyperparameters found with both approaches is different, but their Balanced Accuracy is identical. However, they significantly outperform the default.
    • Values:
      • RandomizedSearch: {'n_neighbors': 2, 'weights': 'distance'} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.8624)
      • GridSearch: {'n_neighbors': 1, 'weights': 'uniform'} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.8624)
      • Default: {'n_neighbors': 5, 'weights': 'uniform'} (Balanced Accuracy: 0.5959)
    • Computational Cost: Again, this RandomizedSearch implementation took longer than GridSearch (1.25 seconds instead of 0.48 seconds) because we try more alternatives (50 candidates instead of 14).

  • The plots reveal the same trends identified with Grid Search:
    • Decision Tree: The tree benefits from a lower value of Min Samples Split and a higher Max Depth, although the performance does not change with Max Depth when Min Samples Split is 2.
    • KNN: The algorithm improves when the Number of Neighbors (k) is smaller. Using Distance Weights is generally better than using Uniform Weights, although both approaches have the same performance when k = 1 or k = 2.

c. Optuna Optimization:¶

Optuna leverages Bayesian optimization to efficiently search for hyperparameter configurations that maximize the Balanced Accuracy. Unlike exhaustive methods such as GridSearchCV or random sampling as in RandomizedSearchCV, Optuna uses a guided approach to prioritize promising areas of the parameter space. This makes it computationally efficient and effective for large parameter spaces.

Implementation:

  • Parameter Search Space:

    • Decision Tree:

      • max_depth: Integer values sampled between 5 and 50.

      • min_samples_split: Integer values sampled between 2 and 20.

    • KNN:

      • n_neighbors: Integer values sampled between 1 and 20.

      • weights: Categorical choices between uniform and distance.

  • Execution Steps:

    • Number of Trials: A total of 50 trials are executed for each model.

    • Search Strategy: Optuna's Bayesian optimization balances exploration and exploitation, focusing on areas of the parameter space with the most potential for improvement.

    • Scoring Metric: balanced_accuracy is chosen as the evaluation metric to account for class imbalance.

In [26]:
import importlib
import subprocess
import sys

# Check if the library is installed
try:
    importlib.import_module('optuna')
    print("Optuna is already installed.")
except ImportError:
    print("Optuna not found. Installing...")
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "optuna"])

import optuna
from optuna.samplers import RandomSampler
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score


def objective_dt(trial):
    """Objective function for Decision Tree."""
    max_depth = trial.suggest_int('max_depth', 5, 50)
    min_samples_split = trial.suggest_int('min_samples_split', 2, 20)
    model = Pipeline(steps=[
        ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
        ('classifier', DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=max_depth, min_samples_split=min_samples_split,
                                              random_state=STUDENT_ID))
    ])
    cv_results = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=inner, scoring='balanced_accuracy')
    return cv_results.mean()


def objective_knn(trial):
    """Objective function for KNN."""
    n_neighbors = trial.suggest_int('n_neighbors', 1, 20)
    weights = trial.suggest_categorical('weights', ['uniform', 'distance'])
    model = Pipeline(steps=[
        ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
        ('classifier', KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=n_neighbors, weights=weights))
    ])
    cv_results = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=inner, scoring='balanced_accuracy')
    return cv_results.mean()


models_optuna = {
    'Decision Tree + Optuna': objective_dt,
    'KNN + Optuna': objective_knn
}
results_optuna = dict()
for model_name, objective in models_optuna.items():
    n_trials = 50
    study = optuna.create_study(direction='maximize', sampler=RandomSampler(seed=STUDENT_ID))
    start_time = time.perf_counter()
    study.optimize(objective, n_trials=n_trials)
    exec_time = time.perf_counter() - start_time
    results_optuna[model_name] = {
        'Balanced Accuracy (mean)': study.best_value,
        'Number of Candidates': n_trials,
        'Execution Time': exec_time,
        'Best Parameters': study.best_params,
        'Optuna Study': study
    }
print_results(results_optuna)

Results:

Optuna evaluates 50 trials for each model. The best-performing configurations and their corresponding Balanced Accuracy and execution times are as follows:

Model Number of Candidates Best Parameters Balanced Accuracy (mean) Execution Time
Decision Tree (Default) {'max_depth': None, 'min_samples_split': 2} 0.8128 ± 0.0134 0.03 seconds
KNN (Default) {'n_neighbors': 5, 'weights': 'uniform'} 0.5959 ± 0.0087 0.01 seconds
Decision Tree + GridSearch 12 {'max_depth': 20, 'min_samples_split': 2} 0.8128 ± 0.0134 0.59 seconds
KNN + GridSearch 14 {'n_neighbors': 1, 'weights': 'uniform'} 0.8624 ± 0.0123 0.48 seconds
Decision Tree + RandomSearch 50 {'max_depth': 47, 'min_samples_split': 2} 0.8128 +/- 0.0134 1.73 seconds
KNN + RandomSearch 50 {'n_neighbors': 2, 'weights': 'distance'} 0.8624 +/- 0.0123 1.25 seconds
Decision Tree + Optuna 50 {'max_depth': 37, 'min_samples_split': 2} 0.8128 23.05 seconds
KNN + Optuna 50 {'n_neighbors': 1, 'weights': 'distance'} 0.8624 21.93 seconds

Insights:

  • Efficacy: Optuna reaches the optimal hyperparameter values found with the previous methods
  • Efficiency: Optuna requires a significantly higher execution time (23.05 seconds instead of 1.73 seconds for Decision Tree, with the same number of candidates) due to the sophisticated Bayesian optimization method used.

Visualization:

Visualizing the optimization results helps in understanding how Optuna explored the parameter space and identified the best-performing configurations for each model.

Decision Tree:

  1. Balanced Accuracy achieved across all Optuna trials for Decision Tree:
In [27]:
study_dt = results_optuna['Decision Tree + Optuna']['Optuna Study']
dt_trials = study_dt.trials_dataframe()
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(dt_trials.index, dt_trials['value'], marker='o', linestyle='-', color='blue', label='Decision Tree')
plt.axhline(y=study_dt.best_value, color='green', linestyle='--', label='Best Balanced Accuracy')
plt.xlabel('Trial Number')
plt.ylabel('Balanced Accuracy')
plt.title('Optuna Optimization: Decision Tree')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
  1. Hyperparameter scatter plot for Decision Tree:
In [28]:
study_dt = results_optuna['Decision Tree + Optuna']['Optuna Study']
trials = study_dt.trials_dataframe()
    
# Extract parameters and scores
param_max_depth = trials["params_max_depth"]
param_min_samples_split = trials["params_min_samples_split"]
mean_test_scores = trials["value"]

# Create a scatter plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
scatter = plt.scatter(param_min_samples_split, param_max_depth, c=mean_test_scores, cmap='viridis', marker='o')
plt.title('Decision Tree Balanced Accuracy (2D Plot)')
plt.xlabel('Min Samples Split')
plt.ylabel('Max Depth')
plt.colorbar(scatter, label='Balanced Accuracy')
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

Insights:

  • Optuna trials plot:
    • The Balanced Accuracy fluctuates significantly across the trials as Optuna explores the parameter space.
    • Optuna progressively identifies better configurations as trials progress.
    • Optuna balances exploration and exploitation; sudden drops in Balanced Accuracy reflect exploratory trials.
  • Hyperparameter scatter plot:
    • Compared with the uniform plot of RandomizedSearch, we see Optuna tends to try higher values of Max Depth after noticing it improves model performance.

study_knn = results_optuna['KNN + Optuna']['Optuna Study']
trials = study_knn.trials_dataframe()
    
# Extract parameters and scores
param_n_neighbors = trials["params_n_neighbors"]
param_weights = trials["params_weights"]
mean_test_scores = trials["value"]

results_knn = pd.DataFrame({
    'n_neighbors': param_n_neighbors,
    'weights': param_weights,
    'mean_test_score': mean_test_scores
})

# Separate results by weight type
uniform_scores = results_knn[results_knn['weights'] == 'uniform']
distance_scores = results_knn[results_knn['weights'] == 'distance']

# Plot the results
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(uniform_scores['n_neighbors'], uniform_scores['mean_test_score'], label='Uniform Weights', marker='o')
plt.scatter(distance_scores['n_neighbors'], distance_scores['mean_test_score'], label='Distance Weights', marker='o')
plt.title('Balanced Accuracy for kNN Hyperparameters')
x_min = int(results_knn['n_neighbors'].min())
x_max = int(results_knn['n_neighbors'].max())
plt.xticks(range(x_min, x_max + 1, 2))
plt.xlabel('Number of Neighbors (k)')
plt.ylabel('Balanced Accuracy')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

Insights:

  • Optuna trials plot:
    • Optuna initially tests less favorable parameter combinations.
    • However, it quickly finds the optimal hyperparameter combination after a few trials.
  • Hyperparameter scatter plot:
    • After noticing that Distance Weights and a low value for the Number of Neighbors improve performance, Optuna tests multiple trials in this region of the search space.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_method_comparison(results, models_order=None, methods_order=None):
    # Treat "Default" as a method for comparison
    results = {k if len(k.split(" + ")) > 1 else f"{k} + Default": v for k, v in results.items()}

    # Extract models, methods, and accuracies
    base_models = set(key.split(" + ")[0] for key in results.keys())
    methods = set(key.split(" + ")[1] for key in results.keys())
    
    grouped_results = {model: {} for model in base_models}
    for key, value in results.items():
        model, method = key.split(" + ")
        grouped_results[model][method] = value['Balanced Accuracy (mean)']
    
    # Plot setup
    if models_order:
        base_models = [x for x in base_models if x in models_order]
        base_models = sorted(base_models, key=lambda x: models_order.index(x))
    else:
        base_models = sorted(base_models)
    if methods_order:
        methods = [x for x in methods if x in methods_order]
        methods = sorted(methods, key=lambda x: methods_order.index(x))
    else:
        methods = sorted(methods)
    x = np.arange(len(base_models))  # Base model positions
    
    # Dynamic bar width and offsets
    total_width = 0.8  # Total width allocated for bars at each x position
    num_methods = len(methods)
    width = total_width / num_methods  # Width of each bar
    offsets = np.linspace(-total_width / 2 + width / 2, total_width / 2 - width / 2, num_methods)
    
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
    
    for offset, method in zip(offsets, methods):
        means = [grouped_results[model].get(method, 0) for model in base_models]
        ax.bar(x + offset, means, width, label=method)
    
    # Formatting the plot
    ax.set_xlabel('Base Models')
    ax.set_ylabel('Balanced Accuracy (mean)')
    ax.set_title('Comparison of Balanced Accuracy by Method')
    ax.set_xticks(x)
    ax.set_xticklabels(base_models, rotation=45)
    ax.legend(title='Method')
    ax.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
    
    # Annotate each bar with its value
    for offset, method in zip(offsets, methods):
        means = [grouped_results[model].get(method, 0) for model in base_models]
        for i, mean in enumerate(means):
            if mean > 0:
                ax.text(x[i] + offset, mean + 0.01, f'{mean:.2f}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

plot_method_comparison(
    {**results_default, **results_gridsearch, **results_randomsearch, **results_optuna},
    models_order=['Dummy', 'Decision Tree', 'KNN'],
    methods_order=['Default', 'GridSearch', 'RandomSearch', 'Optuna']
)

Conclusions:

  • Does HPO improve results over default hyperparameter values? Yes, HPO significantly improves results for the KNN model but not for the Decision Tree:

    • For KNN, the Balanced Accuracy improved from 0.5959 ± 0.0087 with default parameters to 0.8624 ± 0.0123 with HPO (using any method).
    • For the Decision Tree, the Balanced Accuracy remained unchanged at 0.8128 ± 0.0134, indicating that the default hyperparameters were already optimal or close to optimal for this dataset.

  • At what computational cost? The computational cost of HPO varies by method:

    • GridSearch: Moderate computational cost. For Decision Tree, it took 0.59 seconds; for KNN, 0.48 seconds. This method tested all combinations of a predefined grid.
    • RandomSearch: Higher computational cost due to a larger number of candidates (50). It required 1.73 seconds for the Decision Tree and 1.25 seconds for KNN.
    • Optuna: The most computationally expensive method, requiring 23.05 seconds for Decision Tree and 21.93 seconds for KNN, despite evaluating the same number of candidates as RandomSearch (50). This cost reflects Optuna's advanced optimization strategies.

  • Which HPO technique obtains the best results?

    • All HPO techniques achieved the same Balanced Accuracy for each model:
      • For Decision Tree: No improvement over default parameters (0.8128 ± 0.0134).
      • For KNN: Significant improvement to 0.8624 ± 0.0123, regardless of HPO technique.
    • However, GridSearch achieved the same results as the other techniques with lower computational cost, making it the most efficient choice for this dataset and set of hyperparameters.

4. Addressing Class Imbalance with SMOTE and Class Weights¶

4.1 Introduction¶

Class imbalance is a common challenge in machine learning, where the disproportionate representation of classes leads to biased models favoring the majority class. To address this issue, two standard techniques are explored:

  • SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique): Generates synthetic samples for the minority class to balance the dataset.

  • Class Weights: Adjusts the penalty for misclassification of each class based on its frequency, giving higher importance to the minority class.

This section evaluates the impact of these methods on two classifiers, Decision Tree and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), using metrics such as Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, and Confusion Matrix. The goal is to assess whether these techniques improve results and identify the most effective approach.

Methodology:

  1. Dataset Preprocessing: the preprocessing pipeline defined before (imputation, scaling, one-hot and ordinal encoding).

  2. Techniques for Addressing Class Imbalance:

    • SMOTE:

      • Implemented using the imblearn library.

      • Synthetic samples are generated for the minority class.

    • Class Weights:

      • Decision Tree: Class weights are applied natively by setting class_weight='balanced'.

      • KNN: Sample weights are calculated using compute_sample_weight from sklearn.utils.class_weight.

  3. Metrics and Evaluation:The models are evaluated using:

    • Balanced Accuracy: To account for class imbalance.
    • Accuracy: Overall correctness of predictions.
    • Confusion Matrix: For detailed class-wise performance analysis.
    • Execution Time: To assess computational efficiency.

  4. Experimental Setup:

    • Seed: The student ID ensures reproducibility.
    • Inner Evaluation: The models are evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation in the training data.

4.2 SMOTE¶

SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) is implemented as part of the preprocessing pipeline to address class imbalance by generating synthetic samples for the minority class. This ensures both the Decision Tree and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) models are trained on balanced data, potentially improving their ability to generalize.

In [32]:
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE

# SMOTE pipelines for Decision Tree and KNN
smote_models = {
    'Decision Tree + SMOTE': ImbPipeline(steps=[
        ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
        ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=STUDENT_ID)),
        ('classifier', DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))
    ]),
    'KNN + SMOTE': ImbPipeline(steps=[
        ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
        ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=STUDENT_ID)),
        ('classifier', KNeighborsClassifier())
    ])
}

# Dictionary to store results
results_smote = {}

for model_name, model in smote_models.items():
    accuracy_scores = []
    balanced_accuracy_scores = []
    fit_times = []
    conf_matrices = []

    # Perform stratified 5-fold cross-validation
    for i, (train_index, test_index) in enumerate(inner.split(X_train, y_train)):
        X_train_fold, X_test_fold = X_train.iloc[train_index], X_train.iloc[test_index]
        y_train_fold, y_test_fold = y_train.iloc[train_index], y_train.iloc[test_index]

        # Apply SMOTE on the training fold
        start_time = time.perf_counter()
        model.fit(X_train_fold, y_train_fold)
        fit_times.append(time.perf_counter() - start_time)

        # Predict and evaluate on the validation fold
        y_pred = model.predict(X_test_fold)
        balanced_accuracy = balanced_accuracy_score(y_test_fold, y_pred)
        accuracy_scores.append(np.mean(y_test_fold == y_pred))
        balanced_accuracy_scores.append(balanced_accuracy)
        conf_matrices.append(confusion_matrix(y_test_fold, y_pred))
        print(f"Model: {model_name} | Fold {i+1} | Balanced accuracy: {balanced_accuracy:.4f}")

    # Aggregate results
    results_smote[model_name] = {
        'Accuracy (mean)': np.mean(accuracy_scores),
        'Accuracy (std)': np.std(accuracy_scores),
        'Balanced Accuracy (mean)': np.mean(balanced_accuracy_scores),
        'Balanced Accuracy (std)': np.std(balanced_accuracy_scores),
        'Fit Time (mean)': np.mean(fit_times),
        'Fit Time (std)': np.std(fit_times),
        'Confusion Matrix': np.sum(conf_matrices, axis=0)  # Aggregate confusion matrices across folds
    }

Insights:

  1. Accuracy:

    • The Decision Tree + SMOTE model achieved the highest accuracy (0.9022), marginally outperforming the Decision Tree (Default) (0.9005). This indicates that the inclusion of SMOTE improves performance slightly by addressing class imbalance.
    • The KNN (Default) model (0.8478) performed better than the KNN + SMOTE model (0.7066). This suggests that SMOTE may not be as effective for the KNN algorithm in terms of overall accuracy.

  2. Balanced Accuracy:

    • The Decision Tree + SMOTE model has the highest balanced accuracy (0.8286), indicating that it performs well across both majority and minority classes. This improvement is likely due to SMOTE balancing the dataset.
    • The KNN + SMOTE model shows improved balanced accuracy (0.7761) compared to KNN (Default) (0.5959). Although its overall accuracy dropped, the better balanced accuracy suggests it is less biased towards the majority class.

  3. Fit Time:

    • The Decision Tree + SMOTE model takes the longest to fit (0.0), reflecting the additional computational cost of using SMOTE.
    • The KNN + SMOTE model has a fit time of 0.03 seconds, which is slightly longer than the KNN (Default) (0.01 seconds) but still relatively fast.
    • The Dummy and KNN (Default) models have the shortest fit times, indicating they are computationally lightweight but may sacrifice predictive power.

  4. Trade-offs:

    • While SMOTE enhances the balanced accuracy for both models, the impact on overall accuracy and fit time varies. For Decision Tree, the trade-off is minimal, making it a strong candidate for imbalanced datasets.
    • For KNN, SMOTE improves class balance at the cost of a significant drop in overall accuracy, suggesting that alternative techniques might be more effective for handling imbalance in KNN.

Confusion Matrices:

To understand the impact of SMOTE on the Decision Tree's and KNN's performance, we can plot their confusion matrices:

In [35]:
plot_confusion_matrix(

Additional Insights from Confusion Matrices:

  1. Dummy Model:

    • The confusion matrix for the Dummy Model shows that it predicts only the majority class (0) and completely ignores the minority class (1).
    • All instances of the minority class are misclassified, which is reflected in its balanced accuracy of 0.5, as it only performs well on the majority class.

  2. Decision Tree (Default):

    • The Decision Tree (Default) achieves a good balance between the classes, with 1859 correctly classified majority class instances (0) and 259 correctly classified minority class instances (1).
    • However, it misclassifies 120 minority class instances as the majority class, showing room for improvement in handling minority class predictions.

  3. KNN (Default):

    • The KNN (Default) model performs very well on the majority class (1909 correctly classified) but struggles with the minority class, misclassifying 294 minority instances and correctly classifying only 85.
    • This imbalance reflects in its lower balanced accuracy of 0.5959, suggesting that it is biased towards the majority class.

  4. Decision Tree + SMOTE:

    • The Decision Tree + SMOTE model shows an improvement in correctly classifying the minority class, with 273 instances correctly predicted compared to 259 in the default version.
    • However, it slightly increases the number of misclassifications for the majority class (124 compared to 114 in the default version), a typical trade-off when using SMOTE to address class imbalance.

  5. KNN + SMOTE:

    • The KNN + SMOTE model has the most significant shift in behavior. While it improves the correct classification of the minority class (333 correctly classified compared to 85 in the default version), it significantly sacrifices the performance on the majority class (1329 correctly classified compared to 1909).
    • The high number of false positives for the minority class indicates that SMOTE may have led to overfitting or noise in the data for this model.

General Observations:

  • SMOTE consistently improves the classification of the minority class for both the Decision Tree and KNN models, as evident from the increased true positives (1 predictions).
  • However, the trade-off for using SMOTE is evident in the increased number of false positives for the majority class, with a more pronounced effect in the KNN model.
  • The Decision Tree + SMOTE strikes a better balance between majority and minority class predictions compared to the KNN + SMOTE, which suffers from significant performance loss on the majority class.

4.3 Class Weights¶

Class Weights are integrated to address class imbalance by adjusting the penalty for misclassifications. For Decision Tree, the class_weight='balanced' parameter ensures that the minority class receives a higher penalty, encouraging the model to treat both classes more equally. For KNN, scikit-learn does not support class weights.

In [36]:

        start_time = time.perf_counter()
        model.fit(X_train_fold, y_train_fold)
        fit_times.append(time.perf_counter() - start_time)
        y_pred = model.predict(X_test_fold)

        balanced_accuracy = balanced_accuracy_score(y_test_fold, y_pred)
        accuracy_scores.append(np.mean(y_test_fold == y_pred))
        balanced_accuracy_scores.append(balanced_accuracy)
        conf_matrices.append(confusion_matrix(y_test_fold, y_pred))

    }

4.4 Conclusions¶

We evaluated SMOTE and Class Weights, applied to Decision Tree and KNN classifiers, with the following results:

  1. Decision Tree:

    • SMOTE improved both overall accuracy and balanced accuracy, indicating enhanced performance for the minority class with minimal trade-offs in computational efficiency.
    • Class Weights, however, provided no significant improvement over the default configuration, suggesting its limited utility in this context.

  2. KNN:

    • While SMOTE increased balanced accuracy, it caused a significant drop in overall accuracy.

  3. Trade-offs:

    • SMOTE generally improves class balance at the cost of increased computational time, especially for Decision Tree. For KNN, the trade-off includes a decline in overall prediction accuracy.
    • Class Weights are computationally efficient but do not enhance performance in this dataset.

Overall, Decision Tree with SMOTE emerged as the most effective combination.

Are Results Improved?

Yes, results are improved, particularly for the Decision Tree model with SMOTE, which showed enhancements in both overall accuracy and balanced accuracy. For KNN, SMOTE improved balanced accuracy but at the cost of reduced overall accuracy. Class Weights did not significantly improve performance for Decision Trees.

4.5 Techniques for Imbalance and HPO¶

In this final section, we evaluate the performance of techniques for imbalance in combination with HPO:

  • Technique for Imbalance: We choose SMOTE as opposed to Class Weights because:
    • It can be applied to both Decision Trees and KNN, making the implementation easier.
    • It gave better results for Decision Trees.
  • HPO Method: We choose GridSearch as opposed to RandomizedSearch or Optuna because:
    • It successfully reached the optimal hyperparameters in our previous experiments.
    • Using a limited search space, it was more computationally efficient than the other methods.
In [40]:
# SMOTE + GridSearch Pipelines for Decision Tree and KNN
smote_gridsearch_models = {
    'Decision Tree + SMOTE & GridSearch': (
        ImbPipeline(steps=[
            ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
            ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=STUDENT_ID)),
            ('classifier', DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))
        ]),
        {'classifier__max_depth': [10, 20, 30, None],

    ),

            ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
            ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=STUDENT_ID)),

        {'classifier__n_neighbors': list(range(1, 8, 1)),

    )
}

# Dictionary to store results
results_smote_gridsearch = {}

for model_name, (model, param_grid) in smote_gridsearch_models.items():
    grid_search = GridSearchCV(model, param_grid, cv=inner, scoring='balanced_accuracy', n_jobs=-1, verbose=1)
    
    start_execution = time.perf_counter()
    grid_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    execution_time = time.perf_counter() - start_execution
    
    cv_results = grid_search.cv_results_
    best_index = grid_search.best_index_
    
    results_smote_gridsearch[model_name] = {
        'Balanced Accuracy (mean)': cv_results['mean_test_score'][best_index],
        'Balanced Accuracy (std)': cv_results['std_test_score'][best_index],
        'Fit Time (mean)': cv_results['mean_fit_time'][best_index],
        'Fit Time (std)': cv_results['std_fit_time'][best_index],
        'Number of Candidates': len(cv_results['params']),
        'Execution Time': execution_time,
        'Best Parameters': grid_search.best_params_,
    }
    print(f"Model: {model_name} | Best Balanced Accuracy: {cv_results['mean_test_score'][best_index]:.4f}")

5. Advanced Methods for Improved Predictive Performance: Bagging and Boosting¶

5.1 Bagging and Boosting With Default Configuration¶

Advanced ensemble methods, such as bagging and boosting, are highly effective for improving predictive performance. This section evaluates the performance of two chosen advanced methods:

  1. Bagging Technique: Random Forest, selected because it has inherent support for handling class imbalance using class weights (built-in class_weight='balanced'), which will be used later.

  2. Boosting Technique: XGBoost, chosen because it handles numerical features really well, which account for 75% of the features in our dataset (alternatives like catboost are not necessary).

Methodology:

  1. Dataset Preprocessing:

    • Random Forest: the preprocessing pipeline defined before (imputation, scaling, one-hot and ordinal encoding).
    • XGBoost: the same preprocessing pipeline, with an additional step to encode the target variable with numbers (0 and 1 instead of 'No' and 'Yes') using LabelEncoder, as required by the xgboost library.

  2. Techniques for Class Imbalance: we will use no techniques at first.

  3. Hyperparameter Tuning Methods: we will use no hyperparameter tuning at first.

  4. Evaluation Metrics:

    • Balanced Accuracy: Primary metric to assess performance on imbalanced datasets.

    • Accuracy: Overall prediction correctness.

    • Confusion Matrix: Class-wise evaluation of predictions.

    • Execution Time: Measures computational efficiency for practical application.

  5. Experimental Setup:

    • Reproducibility: Ensured using a fixed seed derived from the student ID.

    • Inner Evaluation: The models are evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation in the training data.

  6. Comparison: The methods will be compared with:

    • The Dummy model, the Decision Tree classifier and the kNN algorithm with default hyperparameters.
    • The Decision Tree classifier and the kNN algorithm with SMOTE & GridSearch, our best-performing models so far.
In [43]:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

# Define Random Forest with default configuration
rf_pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', RandomForestClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))
])

# Define XGBoost pipeline with LabelEncoder
class XGBoostPipeline(Pipeline):
    def fit(self, X, y):
        # Encode labels for XGBoost
        self.label_encoder = LabelEncoder()
        y_encoded = self.label_encoder.fit_transform(y)
        return super().fit(X, y_encoded)
    
    def predict(self, X):
        # Get numeric predictions and convert back to original labels
        numeric_predictions = super().predict(X)
        return self.label_encoder.inverse_transform(numeric_predictions)

xgb_pipeline = XGBoostPipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', XGBClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))
])

models = {'Random Forest': rf_pipeline, 'XGBoost': xgb_pipeline}
results_ensembles_default = dict()
for model_name, model in models.items():
    accuracy_scores = []
    balanced_accuracy_scores = []
    fit_times = []
    conf_matrices = []
    
    # Perform stratified 5-fold cross-validation
    for i, (train_index, test_index) in enumerate(inner.split(X_train, y_train)):
        X_train_fold, X_test_fold = X_train.iloc[train_index], X_train.iloc[test_index]
        y_train_fold, y_test_fold = y_train.iloc[train_index], y_train.iloc[test_index]
        
        # Record fit time
        start_time = time.time()
        model.fit(X_train_fold, y_train_fold)
        fit_times.append(time.time() - start_time)
        
        # Predict and evaluate
        y_pred = model.predict(X_test_fold)
        balanced_accuracy = balanced_accuracy_score(y_test_fold, y_pred)
        accuracy_scores.append(np.mean(y_test_fold == y_pred))
        balanced_accuracy_scores.append(balanced_accuracy)
        conf_matrices.append(confusion_matrix(y_test_fold, y_pred))
        print(f"Model: {model_name} | Fold {i+1} | Balanced accuracy: {balanced_accuracy:.4f}")
    
    # Aggregate results
    results_ensembles_default[model_name] = {
        'Accuracy (mean)': np.mean(accuracy_scores),
        'Accuracy (std)': np.std(accuracy_scores),
        'Balanced Accuracy (mean)': np.mean(balanced_accuracy_scores),
        'Balanced Accuracy (std)': np.std(balanced_accuracy_scores),
        'Fit Time (mean)': np.mean(fit_times),
        'Fit Time (std)': np.std(fit_times),
        'Confusion Matrix': np.sum(conf_matrices, axis=0)  # Aggregate confusion matrices across folds
    }

5.2 Bagging and Boosting With Class Imbalance Techniques¶

Techniques for Class Imbalance:

  • Random Forests: We will test three alternatives:
    • Default, with no imbalance techniques.
    • The built-in class_weight='balanced' to penalize misclassification based on class frequency.
    • The SMOTE method.
  • XGBoost: We will test two alternatives:
    • Default, with no imbalance techniques.
    • The SMOTE method.
In [47]:
# Define Random Forest with class weights
rf_weights_pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', RandomForestClassifier(
        class_weight='balanced',
        random_state=STUDENT_ID
    ))
])

# Define Random Forest + SMOTE
rf_smote_pipeline = ImbPipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=STUDENT_ID)),
    ('classifier', RandomForestClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))
])

# Define XGBoost + SMOTE with LabelEncoder
class XGBoostSMOTEPipeline(ImbPipeline):
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.label_encoder = LabelEncoder()
        y_encoded = self.label_encoder.fit_transform(y)
        return super().fit(X, y_encoded)
    
    def predict(self, X):
        numeric_predictions = super().predict(X)
        return self.label_encoder.inverse_transform(numeric_predictions)

xgb_smote_pipeline = XGBoostSMOTEPipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=STUDENT_ID)),
    ('classifier', XGBClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))
])

# Define models dictionary

    'XGBoost + SMOTE': xgb_smote_pipeline
}

Insights:

  • Random Forest + Class Weights:
    • Compared to the Default configuration, it has a slightly smaller Accuracy and Balanced Accuracy.
    • Conclusion: using class weights degrades performance in our dataset (the same thing happened with Decision Trees).
  • Random Forest + SMOTE:
    • Looking at the table/barplot, we see using SMOTE considerably improves the Balanced Accuracy and slightly improves the overall Accuracy.
    • Looking at the confusion matrix, we notice the performance boost comes from predicting minority class (class 1) better than before.
    • Conclusion: SMOTE a great technique for Random Forest in this dataset.
  • XGBoost + SMOTE:
    • In this case, the use of SMOTE has minimal negative effects in both Balanced Accuracy and overall Accuracy.
    • Conclusion: SMOTE does not work as well with XGBoost in this dataset.

So far, our best model is XGBoost with Default configuration.

5.3 Bagging and Boosting With HPO¶

Hyperparameter Tuning Methods:

  • Random Forest: We will apply HPO on top of Random Forest + SMOTE, since SMOTE proved to be beneficial in this case.
  • XGBoost: HPO will be applied on top of XGBoost with Default configuration, which is our top-performing model so far.
  • HPO Method:
    • Method: We will use RandomizedSearch since the number of hyperparameters of both algorithms is too large to do an exhaustive grid search.
    • Number of Candidates:
      • Random Forest + SMOTE: We will only sample 5 values because this method is significantly slower.
      • XGBoost: We will sample 30 values.

The default values for the hyperparameters are:

In [51]:
print("Random Forest Default Parameters:")
rf = RandomForestClassifier()
print(rf.get_params())

# XGBoost default parameters
# Please refer to https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/parameter.html and https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/stable/python/python_api.html#xgboost.XGBClassifier

Random Forest Default Parameters:
{'bootstrap': True, 'ccp_alpha': 0.0, 'class_weight': None, 'criterion': 'gini', 'max_depth': None, 'max_features': 'sqrt', 'max_leaf_nodes': None, 'max_samples': None, 'min_impurity_decrease': 0.0, 'min_samples_leaf': 1, 'min_samples_split': 2, 'min_weight_fraction_leaf': 0.0, 'monotonic_cst': None, 'n_estimators': 100, 'n_jobs': None, 'oob_score': False, 'random_state': None, 'verbose': 0, 'warm_start': False}

Random Forest Hyperparameter Tests: We will test the following hyperparameter values for Random Forest:

  • n_estimators: Tests between 100 and 499 trees in the forest (default: 100)
  • max_depth: Maximum depth of each tree, testing values from 10 to 99 levels (default: None, meaning nodes are expanded until all leaves are pure or contain less than min_samples_split samples)
  • min_samples_split: Minimum samples required to split an internal node (2-19 samples) (default: 2)
  • min_samples_leaf: Minimum samples required in a leaf node (1-9 samples) (default: 1)
  • max_features: Three strategies for feature selection:
    • 'sqrt': Square root of total features (default for classification)
    • 'log2': Log base 2 of total features
    • None: Use all features (default for regression)
  • smote__k_neighbors: Number of nearest neighbors for SMOTE oversampling (3-9 neighbors)

XGBoost Hyperparameter Tests: We will test the following hyperparameter values for XGBoost:

  • n_estimators: Tests between 100 and 499 boosting rounds (default: 100)
  • max_depth: Maximum tree depth from 3 to 9 (typically shallower than Random Forest) (default: 6)
  • learning_rate: Step size shrinkage from 0.01 to 0.31, controlling impact of each tree (default: 0.3)
  • subsample: Ratio of training instances used for each tree (0.6 to 1.0) (default: 1.0)
  • colsample_bytree: Ratio of features used for each tree (0.6 to 1.0) (default: 1.0)
  • min_child_weight: Minimum sum of instance weight needed in a child node (1-6) (default: 1)
In [52]:
from scipy.stats import randint, uniform

# Define parameter distributions for Random Forest with SMOTE
rf_param_dist = {
    'classifier__n_estimators': randint(100, 500),
    'classifier__max_depth': randint(10, 100),
    'classifier__min_samples_split': randint(2, 20),
    'classifier__min_samples_leaf': randint(1, 10),
    'classifier__max_features': ['sqrt', 'log2', None],
    'smote__k_neighbors': randint(3, 10)
}

# Define parameter distributions for XGBoost (without SMOTE parameters)
xgb_param_dist = {
    'classifier__n_estimators': randint(100, 500),
    'classifier__max_depth': randint(3, 10),
    'classifier__learning_rate': uniform(0.01, 0.3),
    'classifier__subsample': uniform(0.6, 0.4),
    'classifier__colsample_bytree': uniform(0.6, 0.4),
    'classifier__min_child_weight': randint(1, 7)
}

# Define Random Forest pipeline with SMOTE
rf_smote_base = ImbPipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=STUDENT_ID)),
    ('classifier', RandomForestClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))
])

# Define XGBoost pipeline without SMOTE
class XGBoostPipeline(ImbPipeline):
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.label_encoder = LabelEncoder()
        y_encoded = self.label_encoder.fit_transform(y)
        return super().fit(X, y_encoded)
    
    def predict(self, X):
        numeric_predictions = super().predict(X)
        return self.label_encoder.inverse_transform(numeric_predictions)

xgb_base = XGBoostPipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', XGBClassifier(random_state=STUDENT_ID))
])

# Define models with their respective parameter distributions
models_randomsearch = {
    'Random Forest + SMOTE & RandomSearch': (rf_smote_base, rf_param_dist, 5),  # Random Forest is much slower
    'XGBoost + RandomSearch': (xgb_base, xgb_param_dist, 30)
}

# Train and evaluate models with HPO
results_ensembles_randomsearch = dict()
for model_name, (base_pipeline, param_dist, n_iter) in models_randomsearch.items():
    # Create and fit RandomizedSearchCV
    random_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
        estimator=base_pipeline,
        param_distributions=param_dist,
        n_iter=n_iter,
        cv=inner,
        scoring='balanced_accuracy',
        n_jobs=-1,
        random_state=STUDENT_ID,
        return_train_score=True
    )
    
    # Fit the model
    start_time = time.time()
    random_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    execution_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    # Extract results from cv_results_
    cv_results = random_search.cv_results_
    best_index = random_search.best_index_
    results_ensembles_randomsearch[model_name] = {
        'Balanced Accuracy (mean)': cv_results['mean_test_score'][best_index],
        'Balanced Accuracy (std)': cv_results['std_test_score'][best_index],
        'Fit Time (mean)':cv_results['mean_fit_time'][best_index],
        'Fit Time (std)': cv_results['std_fit_time'][best_index],
        'Number of Candidates': len(cv_results['params']),
        'Execution Time': execution_time,
        'Best Parameters': random_search.best_params_,
    }

6. Results and Final Model¶

6.1 Introduction¶

This section summarizes the results of the inner evaluation phase, the selection of the best-performing model, and its application to the competition dataset. Additionally, the deliverables, including the saved model and predictions, are discussed.

6.2 Selection of Final Model¶

The balanced accuracy according to our inner evaluation (stratified 5-fold cross-validation) is:

In [55]:
plot_method_comparison({
    **results_default, ** results_gridsearch, **results_randomsearch, **results_smote, **results_smote_gridsearch,
    **results_ensembles_default, **results_ensembles_imbalance, **results_ensembles_randomsearch
})

As we can see, the best-performing model is XGBoost with RandomizedSearch, reaching a balanced accuracy of 0.88.

6.3 Estimation of Future Performance¶

We can train the model using the whole training data, and then test its predictions on the testing data, to get the estimation of future performance (outer evaluation):

In [56]:
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score, accuracy_score, confusion_matrix

final_model = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=xgb_base,
    param_distributions=xgb_param_dist,
    n_iter=30,
    cv=inner,
    scoring='balanced_accuracy',
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=STUDENT_ID,
    return_train_score=True
)

# Fit the model and measure execution time
start_time = time.time()
final_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
execution_time = time.time() - start_time

# Output the results of the RandomizedSearchCV
print(f"Best Parameters: {final_model.best_params_}")
print(f"Best Cross-Validation Score: {final_model.best_score_}")
print(f"Execution Time: {execution_time:.2f} seconds")

# Testing on the testing data
y_pred = final_model.best_estimator_.predict(X_test)

# Compute evaluation metrics
balanced_acc = balanced_accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
conf_matrix = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)

# Display evaluation metrics
print(f"Balanced Accuracy on Testing Data: {balanced_acc:.2f}")
print(f"Accuracy on Testing Data: {acc:.2f}")
print("Confusion Matrix:")
print(conf_matrix)

# Visualize the confusion matrix
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(conf_matrix, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues', xticklabels=np.unique(y_test), yticklabels=np.unique(y_test))
plt.xlabel('Predicted Labels')
plt.ylabel('True Labels')
plt.title('Confusion Matrix')
plt.show()

6.4 Final Model and Competition Dataset¶

We first retrain the model using all available data:

In [57]:
# Separate features (X) and target (y)
X = data_cleaned.drop(columns='Attrition')  # Features
y = data_cleaned['Attrition']               # Target

# Fit the model and measure execution time
start_time = time.time()
final_model.fit(X , y)
execution_time = time.time() - start_time

# Output the results of the RandomizedSearchCV
print(f"Best Parameters: {final_model.best_params_}")
print(f"Best Cross-Validation Score: {final_model.best_score_}")
print(f"Execution Time: {execution_time:.2f} seconds")
